title: Earthquakes and Volcanoes
tagline: Causes, distribution, measurement and effects of earthquakes, and the structure, types and hazards of volcanoes

sourceNote.boardprep: Original study material written by BoardPrep for the CISCE ICSE Class IX Geography syllabus (official-verified baseline, examination year 2027). Magnitudes and casualty figures quoted for the case examples are the widely published official or scientific estimates, and are given as approximations because the estimates of damage and deaths vary slightly between sources. The school model of two or three narrow earthquake belts is a simplification of modern plate tectonics, and the chapter says so where it matters. No board examination paper was consulted, so every question is original practice and not a previous year question.

learningOutcomes: Define an earthquake and label the focus, the epicentre and the seismic waves.
Explain the main causes of earthquakes and describe their world distribution.
Distinguish clearly between the magnitude and the intensity of an earthquake and state the scales used.
Describe the structure of a volcano, the main types of volcano and the regions in which they occur.
State the hazards of volcanic eruption and give safety precautions for earthquakes and volcanoes.

overview.intro: An earthquake is a sudden movement of the Earth's crust that sends waves through the rock. Almost all earthquakes are caused by the movement of one tectonic plate past another along a fault, and they occur at the same time as volcanoes, because both are the result of the same restless interior. The point inside the crust where the movement begins is the focus, and the point on the surface directly above it is the epicentre. The size of an earthquake is stated in two different ways: magnitude describes the total energy released and is a single value for the whole event, while intensity describes what was actually felt and done at a particular place and so differs from place to place. A volcano is a vent through which molten rock, gas and ash reach the surface, and the shape it takes depends mostly on the viscosity of its lava. Both phenomena are natural, but both are among the deadliest of natural hazards, which is why the study of their causes and of the precautions against them is a required part of the syllabus.

facts.label: Focus
facts.value: The point inside the crust where an earthquake begins; also called the hypocentre

facts.label: Epicentre
facts.value: The point on the surface directly above the focus, where the shaking is strongest

facts.label: Magnitude
facts.value: A measure of the energy released, on the Richter or moment magnitude scale; one value for the whole earthquake

facts.label: Intensity
facts.value: A measure of the effects felt at a place, on the Modified Mercalli scale; it varies with distance from the epicentre

learn.title: Earthquakes: focus, epicentre and seismic waves

blocks.text: An earthquake is a sudden shaking of the Earth's crust caused by the release of energy that has been stored in rock under strain. The rocks on either side of a fault are locked together by friction, and stress builds up until it exceeds the strength of the rock and the rock gives way. The point inside the Earth where the rupture begins is called the focus, or hypocentre. The point on the surface directly above the focus, which is where the shaking is generally strongest, is the epicentre. The energy released travels outwards from the focus through the Earth as seismic waves, which are recorded by an instrument called a seismograph, and the record is called a seismogram.

items.meaning: The point within the Earth's crust where an earthquake originates; also called the hypocentre.
The point on the Earth's surface directly above the focus, where the effects of the earthquake are strongest.
The waves of energy that travel through the Earth from the focus; they include P-waves, S-waves and surface waves.
The instrument that records the arrival of seismic waves and the ground movement they cause.
A smaller earthquake that follows the main shock and is caused by the same fault adjusting after the main rupture.
A series of great ocean waves caused by the sudden displacement of the sea bed, usually by an undersea earthquake.

blocks.caption: Table: the main types of seismic wave
rows: P-waves (primary)
Compressional, pushing and pulling along the line of travel
Fastest; travel through solids, liquids and gases
S-waves (secondary)
Shear, moving the ground at right angles to the line of travel

Surface waves

items: P-waves arrive first and S-waves later, and the gap between them grows with the distance from the epicentre, which is how the distance to a distant earthquake is worked out.
The region close to the epicentre in which the earthquake cannot be felt is called the blind zone.
Earthquakes are common at plate boundaries but can occur within plates as well, along old faults and in areas of volcanic activity.
The energy released by an earthquake also heats the rock along the fault and can melt it, forming a peculiar glassy rock called pseudotachylyte in some faults.
Deep-focus earthquakes, those with a focus below 300 km, occur only in the subducting slabs of the sinking oceanic plates, because rock cannot break by brittle failure at that depth.

blocks.text: The great majority of earthquakes are tectonic, caused by the movement of the great plates that make up the Earth's crust. Where two plates slide past one another, as along the San Andreas Fault, they lock and strain and then slip suddenly. Where a plate is forced beneath another, as along the subduction zones of the Pacific, the strain is released in great shocks and the sinking slab also feeds volcanoes. Earthquakes also accompany volcanic activity, because magma moving through the crust fractures the rock around it, and they can be caused by the collapse of underground cavities, by the loading of large reservoirs of water, and by human activities such as deep mining and underground nuclear tests.

blocks.caption: Table: main causes of earthquakes
rows: Tectonic movement

The 1934 Bihar and Nepal earthquake, magnitude about 8.1
Volcanic activity
Movement of magma and gas fractures the surrounding rock

The Bhakra Dam in Himachal Pradesh, 1967

items: The circum-Pacific belt, or the Pacific Ring of Fire, contains about 80 per cent of the world's earthquakes and is the area where the great Pacific plate meets the surrounding plates.
The second great belt runs from the Mediterranean through the Himalayas and on to Indonesia, and is often called the Alpine or Mediterranean-Himalayan belt.
A third line of weakness follows the mid-ocean ridges and the East African Rift Valley system.

The school description of two narrow belts is a simplification; modern seismology shows that earthquakes also occur along the mid-ocean ridges and within the interiors of plates, for example the New Madrid zone in the United States.
India lies at the meeting of the Indian, Eurasian and Arabian plates, so the Himalayan belt, the Kachchh and the Rann of Kutch regions and the northeast are all seismically active.

items.text: Give a reason why an undersea earthquake can produce a tsunami.
items.note: If the sea bed is displaced suddenly, usually vertically along a fault, the whole column of water above it is lifted or dropped. This disturbance spreads outwards across the ocean as a series of long waves. In deep water the waves are small and travel fast, but near the shore the water shallows, the waves slow down and pile up into a high wall of water.

learn.title: Magnitude and intensity: two different measurements

blocks.text: Magnitude and intensity are often confused, but they answer different questions. Magnitude describes the size of the earthquake itself, that is the total energy released at the focus, and it is a single number for the whole event, so an earthquake has one magnitude however many places feel it. Magnitude is measured on the Richter scale, devised in 1935, which is logarithmic: a whole number on the scale means about thirty times more energy than the number below it, and the energy increases by roughly ten times for each whole number. Modern seismologists usually quote the moment magnitude scale, which is more reliable for very large earthquakes. Intensity describes the effects at a particular place, that is how much the earthquake was felt and how much damage it did, and it is measured on the Modified Mercalli scale.

items: A shallow earthquake of the same energy as a deep one causes much more damage at the surface because the waves have travelled less distance and lost less energy.
Soft alluvial soil, such as that of the Gangetic plain, amplifies the shaking, while solid rock does not.

An earthquake of magnitude 6 may cause severe damage to old and poorly built houses and little damage to well-designed ones, so the damage depends on the vulnerability of the buildings as well as on the size of the shock.
An aftershock is smaller than the main shock, but it can bring down buildings already weakened by the main shock, so they must not be re-entered.

learn.title: Effects of earthquakes and safety precautions

blocks.text: The damage done by an earthquake depends on its magnitude, its depth, the distance of the place from the epicentre and the strength of the buildings. Fires are a frequent cause of loss of life, because the mains gas and electricity are damaged and a ruptured pipe may ignite. Landslides and rockfalls block roads and railways and cut off hill settlements. Where unconsolidated waterlogged soil is shaken, it loses its strength and behaves like a liquid, a phenomenon called liquefaction, and buildings sink and tilt. Tsunamis devastate coastal settlements. In the developed world most deaths are caused by the collapse of buildings and by the fires that follow, so construction standards matter more than the size of the shock.

items.meaning: The loss of strength of waterlogged unconsolidated soil when it is shaken, so that it behaves like a liquid and foundations fail.
An area in which earthquakes are frequent because of the weakness of the crust along a plate boundary or a fault.
The frequency and distribution of earthquakes in a region.
The standard safety response during shaking: drop to the ground, cover the head and neck, and hold on to solid furniture until the shaking stops.

items: Before an earthquake: build to seismic codes, tie tall furniture and shelves to the walls, keep heavy objects on lower shelves, learn the Drop, Cover, Hold On drill and the local evacuation routes, and keep a torch, a whistle and a stocked first-aid box.

During an earthquake: drop to the ground, cover the head and neck and hold on to solid furniture; stay away from windows, heavy cupboards and hanging objects; if you are outdoors move to an open place away from buildings and power lines; do not use a lift.
After an earthquake: check for injuries and fire, be prepared for aftershocks, do not enter a damaged building even if it looks stable, and do not use the telephone except in an emergency.
If you are near the coast and the sea water suddenly recedes, move inland and uphill at once, because this is the warning that a tsunami has been generated.
An earthquake of magnitude 6 or more should be reported to the nearest police station or the disaster management authority, and the area cordoned off until it is declared safe.

items.text: Why were so many people killed in the Gujarat earthquake of 26 January 2001?
items.note: The earthquake had a magnitude of about 7.7 and its epicentre lay near Bhuj in Kutch, so the shaking was severe in the Rann of Kutch and in the towns around it. More than 20,000 people died and about a million houses were damaged. The main reason for the very high death toll was that many of the buildings, especially in the towns, were not designed to the seismic code and were of heavy unreinforced masonry and multi-storeyed construction, which collapses completely when the ground shakes. The disaster therefore became the starting point of the national programme to rebuild towns under proper seismic design.

blocks.text: A volcano is a vent or fissure through which magma, gases and solid material reach the surface of the Earth. Below the surface the magma collects in a chamber or reservoir, and from it a main vent leads upwards to the crater at the top of the cone. Secondary vents may open on the flanks of the volcano, and they often build small parasitic cones. The material that comes out includes lava, which is the molten rock that flows out, and a great quantity of solid material, including volcanic ash, cinders, pumice and lapilli, together with steam and other gases such as sulphur dioxide and carbon dioxide.

blocks.caption: Table: parts of a volcano
rows: Magma chamber
The reservoir of molten rock beneath the volcano, in which the gases also collect
Main vent
The pipe or chimney through which magma rises to the surface
Crater
The bowl-shaped depression at the summit, formed around the mouth of the vent
Secondary vent
An opening on the flank of the volcano that may build a parasitic cone
Lava
Molten rock that has reached the surface; it may flow a long way if it is fluid and only a short way if it is viscous
Pyroclastic material
Ash, cinders, pumice and lapilli, thrown out during an explosive eruption

items: Basaltic lava is hot, about 1,100 degrees Celsius, and very fluid, so it flows far and builds gentle slopes.
Andesitic or rhyolitic lava is cooler, about 800 to 1,000 degrees Celsius, and viscous, so it forms steep-sided plugs and domes.
Gas is the main agent of explosive eruption, because the pressure of trapped gas is what shatters the rock.
A nuée ardente, or pyroclastic flow, is a fast-moving cloud of hot gas and ash that descends the flanks of the volcano at great speed and is the most lethal of volcanic hazards.
A lahar is a mudflow of ash and water that forms when heavy rain falls on loose ash and sweeps down the valleys.

learn.title: Types of volcano and where they occur

blocks.text: Volcanoes are classified by their state of activity and by their shape and structure. By activity, a volcano is active if it has erupted in historic times, dormant if it has not erupted for a long time but is still capable of doing so, and extinct if it can no longer erupt. By structure, the main types are the shield volcano, with broad gentle slopes built of fluid basaltic lava; the composite or stratovolcano, with steep slopes built of alternating layers of lava and ash; the simple volcanic cone, formed in a single eruptive episode; and the lava dome, formed of very viscous lava that piles up over the vent. Most of the world's volcanoes lie along the Pacific Ring of Fire, and other groups lie in the Mediterranean region, in the East Indies, in the Andes and along the East African Rift Valley.

items: The Pacific Ring of Fire carries about 75 per cent of the world's active volcanoes and about 80 per cent of its earthquakes.
The second great region of volcanic activity runs through the Mediterranean and the East Indies, and includes Italy, Greece, Iceland, Indonesia, the Philippines and Japan.
The Andes of South America carry the longest chain of volcanoes in the world, caused by the subduction of the Nazca plate beneath the South American plate.
The East African Rift Valley volcanoes, such as Mount Kilimanjaro and Mount Kenya, lie on a region where the African plate is being split.
Nearly 80 per cent of the world's volcanoes are on the island arcs and the continental margins facing the Pacific Ocean.

learn.title: Volcanic hazards, case examples and safety

blocks.text: The hazards from an eruption depend on what is thrown out and where the people are. Lava flows destroy property and can be walked on after they cool, so they are a danger to land and buildings but rarely kill people directly. Ash fall smothers crops, roofs collapse under the weight, water supplies and machinery are damaged and the ash affects breathing. Pyroclastic flows are far more dangerous, travelling down the flanks at speeds of over 100 kilometres per hour with temperatures of several hundred degrees. Lahars can travel far along valleys and destroy settlements well away from the volcano. Gases such as carbon dioxide can kill people at close quarters, as happened at Lake Nyos in Cameroon in 1986.

items.text: What happened at Mount St Helens in the United States in 1980?
items.note: A minor eruption and a bulge on the north flank had already warned of activity, but the major eruption of 18 May 1980 was unexpected. The north flank of the volcano collapsed in a giant landslide, which released the pressure and produced a lateral blast that flattened 600 square kilometres of forest and killed about 60 people. The summit was lowered by roughly 400 metres, and a new crater was opened in its place. A pyroclastic flow and lahars carried on down the valleys afterwards. The event led to the setting up of a volcano observatory and a system for monitoring and warning around the mountain.

items.text: Why did the eruption of Mount Pinatubo in the Philippines in 1991 affect the weather of the whole world?
items.note: Pinatubo ejected an estimated 20 million tonnes of sulphur dioxide into the stratosphere, where it was converted into sulphate aerosols. These fine particles reflected a small part of the Sun's radiation back to space and so cooled the Earth's surface for about two years, lowering the average temperature of the northern hemisphere by roughly half a degree Celsius. The eruption also affected the weather of the following years through the creation of a lasting aerosol layer.

items: Before an eruption: monitor the volcano with seismographs, tiltmeters and gas sensors, prepare hazard maps and evacuation plans, and rehearse them with the people living in the danger zone.
During an eruption: follow the official evacuation order at once, move away from the volcano and out of the valleys and river beds below it, and protect the head and neck from falling ash.
Keep away from the crater and from the flanks of the volcano, because lava flows, pyroclastic flows and lahars follow the valleys and the gullies.
Wear a mask and goggles in ash fall, keep the nose and mouth covered and stay indoors if the ash is heavy.
After the eruption: expect lahars for several days, as they are triggered by rain on loose ash, so do not cross a muddy river or a debris-filled gully.
A volcanic ash cloud in the upper air can ground aircraft, so airline companies must be informed of an eruption.

P-waves travel fastest through the whole Earth, S-waves travel only through solids, and surface waves travel along the crust and do the most damage to buildings.

figures.caption: Figure: Structure of a volcano
figures.description: Molten rock collects in a magma chamber beneath the volcano and rises through the main vent to the crater. Secondary vents may open on the flanks, and lava, ash and gases are thrown out at the summit.

figures.caption: Figure: The main earthquake belts of the world
figures.description: The greatest concentration lies in the circum-Pacific belt, or Ring of Fire, which runs from the Andes through the Aleutians, Japan and the Philippines to New Zealand. The second belt runs from the Mediterranean through the Himalayas to Indonesia. A third line of weakness follows the mid-ocean ridges and the East African Rift.

keyPoints: An earthquake is a sudden movement of the Earth's crust caused by the release of accumulated strain.
The focus or hypocentre is the point inside the crust where the earthquake starts; the epicentre is the point on the surface directly above it.
P-waves travel through solids, liquids and gases; S-waves travel only through solids; surface waves are the slowest and the most destructive to buildings.
Most earthquakes are caused by the movement of tectonic plates along faults; others accompany volcanic activity or the collapse of underground cavities.
The Pacific Ring of Fire carries about 80 per cent of the world's earthquakes, and the Mediterranean-Himalayan belt is the second great zone.
Magnitude measures the energy released and gives one value for the whole earthquake; intensity measures the effects felt at a place and varies from place to place.
The Richter scale is logarithmic and the Modified Mercalli scale is the scale of intensity.
Damage depends on the magnitude, the depth, the distance from the epicentre, the local soil and above all on how strong the buildings are.
Liquefaction of waterlogged soil causes buildings to sink and tilt during strong shaking.
A volcano has a magma chamber, a main vent and a crater, and it ejects lava, ash, cinders, pumice and gases.
Shield volcanoes have gentle slopes and fluid basaltic lava; composite volcanoes are steep and built of alternating lava and ash layers.
The Ring of Fire carries about 75 per cent of the world's active volcanoes.
Pyroclastic flows are the most lethal volcanic hazard, and lahars can travel far beyond the volcano along valleys.
The safety rule during shaking is Drop, Cover, Hold On, and a receding sea is the warning that a tsunami has been generated.
examFocus: Questions on the difference between magnitude and intensity are common; prepare the four points of difference in the table and give an example of two places feeling the same earthquake differently.
When asked for the causes of earthquakes, give tectonic movement first and then add the volcanic, collapse, reservoir-induced and human causes; the last two earn easy marks.
Case-study questions are usually built around the 2001 Gujarat earthquake or the 1934 Bihar and Nepal earthquake, and they ask for the causes of the damage and the lesson for town planning.
For volcano questions, state the type of volcano, the reason for its shape, the products of the eruption and the hazard that each product creates.
Safety-precaution questions are often set for ten marks; organise the answer as before, during and after, and give a reason for at least one precaution in each part.

The point on the surface directly above the focus.
A wave of energy travelling through the Earth from the focus of an earthquake.

questions.prompt: The point on the Earth's surface directly above the focus of an earthquake is the:
questions.explanation: The epicentre is the point on the surface directly above the focus, and the shaking is generally strongest there. The focus itself is also called the hypocentre.
questions.commonMistake: Answering 'hypocentre', which is the other name for the focus inside the crust.

questions.prompt: The scale used to describe how much an earthquake is felt at a particular place is the:
questions.explanation: The Modified Mercalli scale measures intensity, that is the observed effects at a place. The Richter scale measures magnitude, that is the energy released by the earthquake as a whole.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing the Richter scale, which describes the size of the earthquake rather than its effects at a place.

questions.prompt: A broad volcano with gentle slopes, built almost entirely of fluid basaltic lava, is a:
questions.explanation: A shield volcano is built by long flows of very fluid basaltic lava, so each layer is thin and wide and the slopes stay gentle. A composite volcano has steep sides because it is built of alternating lava and ash layers.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing composite volcano, which is steep-sided and is the type students meet most often, such as Mount Fuji.

questions.prompt: Which of the following seismic waves can travel only through solids?
questions.explanation: S-waves are shear waves and need a rigid medium, so they cannot pass through the liquid outer core. P-waves travel through solids, liquids and gases, and surface waves travel along the surface of the crust.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing P-waves, which are the fastest and the first to arrive but which travel through liquids as well.

questions.prompt: The greatest concentration of the world's volcanoes and earthquakes lies along the:
questions.explanation: The circum-Pacific belt carries about 80 per cent of the world's earthquakes and about 75 per cent of its active volcanoes, because the Pacific plate meets the surrounding plates along this line.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing the Mediterranean coast, which is the second great belt and is far smaller.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: the point inside the Earth's crust where an earthquake originates is called the ________, or the hypocentre.
questions.explanation: The focus is the point of origin of the earthquake, and the epicentre is the point on the surface directly above it.
questions.commonMistake: Writing 'epicentre', which is the surface point rather than the point of origin.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: a fast-moving cloud of hot gas and volcanic ash that descends the flank of a volcano is called a ________.
questions.answer: Pyroclastic flow, also called a nuée ardente
questions.explanation: The pyroclastic flow is the most lethal of all volcanic hazards, travelling down the flanks at great speed and at temperatures of several hundred degrees Celsius.
questions.commonMistake: Answering 'lahar', which is the mudflow formed when rain washes ash down the valleys.

questions.prompt: Distinguish between the magnitude and the intensity of an earthquake, giving two points of difference.
questions.answer: Magnitude describes the energy released by the earthquake at its focus and is a single value for the whole event, so one earthquake has only one magnitude. Intensity describes the effects actually felt and the damage done at a particular place, so the same earthquake has a different intensity in every place where it is felt. Magnitude is measured on the Richter scale or the moment magnitude scale and does not change with distance from the epicentre, while intensity is measured on the Modified Mercalli scale and decreases away from the epicentre. Intensity also depends on the depth of the focus and on the nature of the local soil, and magnitude does not.
questions.explanation: The strongest distinction is one value for the event against a different value for every place, and the scales must be named correctly.
questions.commonMistake: Saying that intensity measures the energy released, which is the definition of magnitude.

questions.prompt: State three causes of earthquakes other than the movement of tectonic plates.
questions.answer: Volcanic activity causes earthquakes because the movement of magma and gas through the crust fractures the surrounding rock, and small shocks often precede an eruption. The collapse of large underground cavities, common in limestone country, causes earthquakes when the roof of the cavity falls in. The filling of a large reservoir loads and stresses the rock beneath the valley floor and produces reservoir-induced seismicity, as happened at the Bhakra Dam in Himachal Pradesh in 1967. Deep mining and underground nuclear explosions also release strain that has built up in the rock.
questions.explanation: Each cause needs the mechanism, and naming a real example of one of them strengthens the answer.
questions.commonMistake: Giving only one cause with no explanation of how it produces stress in the rock.

questions.prompt: Give three safety precautions to be followed before an earthquake strikes.
questions.answer: Buildings should be designed and constructed to the seismic code, with reinforced frames and light roofs, and heavy buildings should be avoided in the high-risk zones. Tall furniture, cupboards, shelves and gas cylinders should be firmly fixed to the walls and heavy objects should be kept on lower shelves so that they cannot fall on people. Everyone should learn the Drop, Cover and Hold On drill, know the exits from the building and the local evacuation routes, and take part in mock drills. An emergency kit with a torch, a whistle, drinking water, a first-aid box and a charged mobile phone should be kept ready, and the local emergency numbers should be known.
questions.explanation: Precautions before an earthquake concern construction, the securing of furniture, training and emergency supplies.
questions.commonMistake: Listing precautions that should be taken during the shaking, which does not answer the question.

questions.prompt: Describe the structure of a volcano and explain how the type of lava it produces shapes the volcano.
questions.answer: Molten rock, or magma, collects below the surface in a chamber in which the gases also accumulate. The magma rises through a main vent and reaches the surface at a crater, which is the bowl-shaped depression around the mouth of the vent. Secondary vents may open on the flanks of the cone and sometimes build small parasitic cones. The shape of the volcano depends on the viscosity of the lava. A fluid basaltic lava, at about 1,100 degrees Celsius, runs a long way before it solidifies, so each flow adds a thin, wide layer and the volcano grows as a broad cone with gentle slopes, as in a shield volcano such as Mauna Loa. A cooler and more viscous andesitic or rhyolitic lava, at about 800 to 1,000 degrees Celsius, solidifies soon after it leaves the vent, so the flows are short and steep and build a tall cone with a summit crater, as in a composite volcano such as Mount Fuji. Very viscous lava may not flow at all and simply pile up over the vent as a rounded lava dome. If the eruptions are violently explosive, ash and cinders add steep layers and the volcano has the classic concave cone shape.
questions.explanation: A full answer describes the parts of the volcano and then links the viscosity of the lava to the resulting shape, with a named example of each type.
questions.commonMistake: Describing the parts of the volcano without explaining how the lava controls the shape, which is the point of the question.

questions.prompt: Explain the dangers to people and property posed by a volcanic eruption, using examples of the hazards of lava, ash and pyroclastic flows.
questions.answer: Lava flows are a danger to land, roads, buildings and forests, and they can even set fires where they meet vegetation, but they move slowly and rarely kill people directly, so most of the danger from lava is to property. Volcanic ash is a finer material that falls over a wide area; it smothers crops, blocks roads and drains, chokes machinery and fouls water supplies, and its weight can collapse the roofs of buildings, while its effect on breathing can make breathing difficult for people with chest complaints. The most lethal hazard is the pyroclastic flow, a cloud of hot gas and ash that rushes down the flanks of the volcano at more than 100 kilometres per hour with temperatures of several hundred degrees; it destroys everything in its path, as the lateral blast and the flows of Mount St Helens in 1980 showed, when about 60 people were killed and 600 square kilometres of forest were flattened. Lahars add to the danger, because rain on loose ash produces mudflows that travel far down the valleys and destroy settlements and bridges well away from the volcano itself.
questions.explanation: The answer should rank the hazards by their effect on people and property and support each with its mechanism and an example.
questions.commonMistake: Treating all volcanic hazards as equally deadly, when lava flows are mainly destructive of property and pyroclastic flows are the ones that kill.

questions.prompt: Two places lie close to each other but one is destroyed by an earthquake of magnitude 6 while the other is hardly disturbed. Examine the reasons for this difference.
questions.answer: The size of the shock is only one of the reasons. Depth matters: a shallow-focus earthquake sends its energy through a short distance of rock and loses much less energy before it reaches the surface, so it does far more damage than a deep-focus earthquake of the same magnitude, and the depth of the focus in India can be as little as a kilometre. Distance from the epicentre matters, because the strength of the shaking falls away with distance, so the place nearer the epicentre is shaken harder. The nature of the ground matters, because unconsolidated, waterlogged alluvium amplifies the shaking and can liquefy, causing buildings to sink and tilt, whereas solid rock transmits the waves with much less amplification. Most important of all are the buildings themselves: an earthquake of magnitude 6 kills mainly where buildings were built of heavy unreinforced masonry, were too tall for their foundations, or were not designed to the seismic code, and leaves buildings of sound design standing. So the difference between the two places may be explained less by the earthquake than by the vulnerability of what was built on it, which is the lesson that the Gujarat earthquake of 26 January 2001 gave, where more than 20,000 people died in buildings that had not been designed for seismic safety.
questions.explanation: The reasoning separates the factors that belong to the earthquake itself from those that belong to the site and the buildings, and shows which is usually decisive.
questions.commonMistake: Giving only the distance from the epicentre and forgetting the depth, the ground conditions and the strength of the buildings.

questions.prompt: Volcanoes and earthquakes occur in the same regions of the world. Explain why, and examine the statement that both are caused only by the movement of tectonic plates.
questions.answer: The two occur together because they share a common cause in most cases: the movement of the plates and the movement of magma in the Earth's interior. Where one plate is forced beneath another, as beneath the Andes or beneath Japan, the sinking slab melts and the magma that is generated rises through the crust, feeding the volcanoes of the island arc while the strain in the same plate boundary is released as great earthquakes. The same is true along the mid-ocean ridges, where the sea floor spreads, new crust forms and volcanoes such as those of Iceland rise above it, and the spreading motion also produces shallow earthquakes. At the same time the two are not identical in their cause, so the statement is only partly true. Earthquakes are also produced by the collapse of underground cavities in limestone, by the loading of large reservoirs such as the Bhakra Dam, by deep mining and by underground nuclear explosions, and by volcanic eruptions themselves, which shake the ground as the magma moves. Volcanoes in turn are not only the product of plate boundaries, because they also occur on hot spots, such as the Hawaiian islands, where a plume of hot material rises from deep within the mantle and produces a chain of volcanoes as the plate moves over it, and along the East African Rift, where the African plate is splitting apart. The soundest conclusion is therefore that both phenomena are largely the surface expression of the restless interior of the Earth, that plate movement is the dominant cause of each, and that neither is the sole cause of the other.
questions.explanation: The answer has to accept the common cause, show where the two differ, and give examples of causes that do not depend on a plate boundary.
questions.commonMistake: Accepting the statement as fully true, without noticing that hot-spot volcanoes and reservoir-induced earthquakes fall outside it.
